0401-1500s.title: Untitled, from Chronological History of the United States
0401-1500s.caption: The four chronological charts included in Elizabeth Palmer Peabody’s Chronological History of the United States (1865), which display the significant events of the 1500s, 1600s, 1700s, and 1800s.
0401-1500s.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Internet Archive.
0401-1500s.digitizedLine: Digitized by the Library of Congress.
0401-1500s.altText:
One of the four chronological charts included in Elizabeth Palmer Peabody’s Chronological History of the United States. This chart shows the significant events of the sixteenth century. The chart is a 10 by 10 grid, for a total of 100 squares, each representing one year of the century. The chart is read from left to right and from top to bottom such that the year 1501 corresponds to the top left square and 1600 corresponds to the bottom right square. Each square is further divided into nine smaller squares, the position of which represents a specific type of event, according to the following key: 
Top left: Battles, Sieges, Beginning of War
Top center: Conquests, Annexations, Unions
Top right: Losses and Disasters
Middle left: Falls of States
Middle center: Foundations of States and Revolutions
Middle right: Treaties and Sundries
Bottom left: Births
Bottom center: Deeds
Bottom right: Deaths, of remarkable individuals
An event is indicated by shading the appropriate sub-square in the appropriate year. The color of the shading indicates the country that is involved. In the chart of the sixteenth century, the chart is mostly unshaded, with only one or two events per row (decade). The most prominent set of events occurs in 1565, in which multiple sub-squares are shaded. There is no key to the colors included in this image.

A historical visual chart titled "Tableau Muet servant aux Exercices Chronologiques et autres de la Méthode dite Polonaise" by A. Jazwinski, published in Paris in 1835. The chart is organized into a 6x4 grid (24 squares in total), each divided further into smaller colored rectangles and squares within a 10x10 grid, representing abstract or coded chronological data. The top row shows empty or nearly empty grids. The second and third rows contain various colorful blocks—pink, blue, orange, red, green, etc.—each arranged differently across the squares.The fourth and fifth rows show more color-block patterns, some with handwritten symbols like the dieses (‡) .The bottom right square includes text that reads TABLEAU MUET
SERVANT aux Exercices Chronologiques et autres de la MÉTHODE DITE POLONAISE Suivie par A. Jazwinski
PARIS
Bailly-Baillière, Éditeur-Libraire
19, Rue Hautefeuille,
1835.
(Lith. d’Aubert.)

0423-willard-temple.title: The Temple of Time
0423-willard-temple.caption: Emma Willard’s perspectival Temple of Time (1846).
0423-willard-temple.creditLine: Image courtesy of the David Rumsey Map Collection, Cartography Associates.
0423-willard-temple.digitizedLine: Digitized by the David Rumsey Map Collection, Cartography Associates.
0423-willard-temple.altText:
A historical chart that depicts a Roman temple in a highly perspectivized, quattrocento style. Each column is labeled with the name of an important ruler. US rulers are in the foreground on the left, and European rulers are in the foreground on the right. Behind those are additional columns with the names of Roman, Greek, and biblical rulers. The columns get smaller as they recede into the back of the chart, indicating that those rulers date earlier in time. At the very back of the temple, written on the wall, are the words “The Creation.”
 
On the ceiling of the temple are the names of additional sets of historical figures: statesmen, philosophers and discoverers, theologicians, poets and painters, and warriors. They are arranged in keeping with the perspectivized style, such that the more contemporary figures appear larger and towards the front, and more historical figures appear smaller and towards the back. On the floor are channels that correspond to different countries, with relevant events written out. A palette of pastel colors separates each country’s channel from the others. These same colors shade the columns and the ceiling, resulting in an overall impression that is visually and textually dense. At this scale, few individual events can be discerned.

0424-Caldas-AJB03_M0514.caption: An elevation profile of Chimborazo, created by the Colombian naturalist Francisco José de Caldas, that likely inspired Humboldt's famous visualization.
0424-Caldas-AJB03_M0514.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Archivo del Real Jardín Botánico, CSIC, Madrid, AJB, Div. III, M529. © Real Jardín Botánico, CSIC.
0424-Caldas-AJB03_M0514.digitizedLine: Digitized by the Real Jardín Botánico
0424-Caldas-AJB03_M0514.notes: Requires copy of book when published. ALso need to write w/ link to low-res images once published.
0424-Caldas-AJB03_M0514.altText:
The image is a hand-drawn cross-section of a mountain range with elevations and ecological zones. It shows a triangular peak (labeled Chimborazo) with horizontal lines marking altitude levels. The mountain profile is drawn in gray, while horizontal color bands in pink and yellow highlight zones of plant growth. The left margin has a vertical table with numbers in Spanish giving altitudes in toises (varas, meters) above sea level.

Text visible on the chart includes (Spanish):
At the top of the mountain: “Chimborazo 3267 to.”

Horizontal labels:
“Término de la Nieve permanente baxo del Equador” (Limit of permanent snow under the Equator).
“Término superior del género Cinchona” (Upper limit of the cinchona genus).
“Término inferior del género Cinchona” (Lower limit of the cinchona genus).

Zones labeled:
“Región del Cultivo” (Region of cultivation).
“Región del Bosque” (Forest region).
Along the base: “Corte de los Andes de Loxa á Oeste a los 4:18 de lat.” (Cross-section of the Andes of Loja to the west at 4°18' latitude).
Lower left corner: “Oceano Pacífico.”

0425-Caldas-AJB03_M0526.caption: [ SEE ABOVE ]
0425-Caldas-AJB03_M0526.altText: This is a historical geological cross-section diagram showing rock formations and strata. The document appears to be from a Spanish or Latin American geological survey, with the title "Nivelacion de las Quintas en gral, y en particular de la de Loya, o, de la Cuechova aficionada por Franco Osse de Caldas." The diagram depicts a mountainous landscape profile with various geological layers represented in different colors including pink, yellow, green, and gray horizontal bands. There are dark formations that appear to be vegetation or rock outcroppings scattered across the terrain. The left side shows a steep mountain slope, while the right side shows more gradual terrain with what appears to be a water body or plain. The document includes measurement scales along the edges and appears to be a professional geological survey document, likely from the 18th or 19th century based on the handwritten Spanish text and artistic style. There are color reference patches visible on the right side of the image, as the document is photographed in an archival setting with measurement rulers for scale reference.

0426-Caldas-AJB03_M0529.altText: A  historical botanical and geographical diagram from the Real Jardín Botánico archives, documenting the Royal Botanical Expedition to the New Kingdom of Granada (1783-1816) directed by José Celestino Mutis. The document is catalogued as AJB, Div. III, M00529. The grayscale image shows a cross-sectional elevation profile of mountains with detailed annotations in Spanish describing the distribution of plant species at different altitudes. The diagram features a mountain range drawn in profile with horizontal grid lines indicating elevation levels. It depicts a cross-sectional view of Mount Chimborazo in Ecuador, showcasing the vertical distribution of plant species along the mountain’s elevation gradient. The central image shows the mountain with detailed annotations of plant names at various altitudes. Flanking the mountain illustration are extensive columns of text and data, including altitude measurements, plant names, and climatic conditions. The title and credits are elegantly handwritten at the bottom in German.

0428-am1829-phelps-67941-d-p1.altText: A historical scientific illustration titled "Top of Chimborazo 21000 feet from the level of the Sea" from Cotopaxi, dated 1836, labeled as Plate 1. The image shows a detailed cross-sectional view of Mount Chimborazo with altitude measurements on the left side (ranging from sea level to 21,000 feet) and latitude measurements on the right side (ranging from 0° to 90° degrees). The mountain is depicted as a triangular peak with extensive text labels covering its surface, indicating different vegetation zones and plant species at various elevations. The illustration uses cross-hatching and shading techniques typical of 19th-century scientific engravings. Clouds are shown around the mountain peak and in the sky. At the bottom of the image is the subtitle "Progress of vegetation at different elevations, corresponding with its progress in different Latitudes."

0429-Willard-4545001.title: Picture of Nations or Perspective Sketch of the Course of Empire,
0429-Willard-4545001.caption: Willard's picture of nations adopts the triangular form of Humboldt's Chimborazo diagram in order to represent the rise and fall of nations.
0429-Willard-4545001.creditLine: Image courtesy of the David Rumsey Map Collection, Cartography Associates.
0429-Willard-4545001.digitizedLine: Digitized by the David Rumsey Map Collection, Cartography Associates.
0429-Willard-4545001.altText: An early 19th-century yellowed historical diagram. The chart is drawn as a three-dimensional perspective view of history, the chart is triangular, tapering toward the top where “CREATION” is inscribed in a cloud. From this point, dark rivers or streams flow downward, splitting, widening, and merging to represent nations and empires across time. The rivers are labeled with names such as “Egyptians,” “Assyrians,” “Hebrews,” “Greeks,” “Romans,” “Empire of Alexander,” “Saracens,” “Turks,” “Spaniards,” “English,” and others. In the center, a radiant sunburst marks the “Empire of Alexander.” Below, a wide, shaded band dominates the middle with the label “ROMAN EMPIRE.” Still farther down, near the base of the triangle, bold text reads “EMPIRE OF NAPOLEON.” On the left edge, the triangular border is marked “ANCIENT HISTORY” near the top, transitioning to “MODERN HISTORY” toward the bottom, with centuries labeled (1st Century, 2nd Century, etc.) all the way through the 19th Century.On the right edge, milestone events are listed, such as: Death of Solomon, Foundation of Rome, Death of Alexander, Birth of Christ, Division of the Roman Empire, Flight of Mahomet, Coronation of Charlemagne, Commencement of the Crusades, Discovery of America, French Revolution. At the very bottom, beneath the triangle, the engraving notes: “Entered according to Act of Congress in the year 1835 by S. H. Huntington of the State of Connecticut.”

0430-priestley-new-chart.title: A New Chart of History
0430-priestley-new-chart.caption: Joseph Priestley’ s widely circulated New Chart of History (1769).
0430-priestley-new-chart.creditLine: Image courtesy of the David Rumsey Map Collection, Cartography Associates.
0430-priestley-new-chart.digitizedLine: Digitized by the David Rumsey Map Collection, Cartography Associates.
0430-priestley-new-chart.notes: Same image appears in Brooks chapter, so don't include here b/c it's a duplicate.
0430-priestley-new-chart.altText: An 18th-century historical timeline chart titled “A New Chart of History” by Joseph Priestley, dedicated to Benjamin Franklin. The chart spans from around 1200 BCE to the late 1700s CE, with time progressing horizontally across the top. Vertical columns represent different civilizations, empires, and regions, with colored bars indicating their duration and prominence. Large labeled areas include “Roman Empire,” “Persians,” “Saracens,” “Franks,” “English,” “French,” “Spaniards,” “Chinese,” “Indians,” “Tartary,” and more. The Roman Empire is depicted as a wide gold-brown block dominating the center. Smaller empires and kingdoms—such as the Parthian Empire, Lombards, Goths, Vandals, Turks, and Normans—are shown as shorter horizontal bands that overlap or succeed one another. At the bottom are lists of rulers and dynasties arranged in sequence. Ornamental cartouche near the left provides an explanation of the chart.

0431-clarke-1-4000BC-ps-30x43-2.title: Chart of Scripture
0431-clarke-1-4000BC-ps-30x43-2.caption: A vertical timeline created by Anne Laura Clarke as it was displayed on her traveling lecture tour, and a second as it was encountered by Granville Ganter in a Clark family attic. (Here the first chart is visible on the left).
0431-clarke-1-4000BC-ps-30x43-2.creditLine: Photo by Granville Ganter. Courtesy of Granville Ganter.
0431-clarke-1-4000BC-ps-30x43-2.altText:
This image shows an antique chronological chart of history, possibly from the 19th century, titled "Chronological Chart of History". The layout is a vertical timeline that organizes various ancient civilizations and empires into parallel colored columns, spanning from 4000 BC to the time of Christ. Some of the major civilizations shown include: Scripture (center, in blue), Egypt, Greece, Rome, Persia, Assyria, China, Syria, Carthage, Macedonia, Lydia, Phoenicia.
Each column represents a civilization, with names and events listed vertically along the timeline. The format allows viewers to compare the rise and fall of civilizations relative to one another in time. The chart is mounted between two wooden rollers, suggesting it was used as a wall chart for educational purposes, likely in a school or scholarly setting.

0437-Peabody-15895000.title: Christan Era
0437-Peabody-15895000.caption: The only extant example of Peabody’s mural charts. This, “Christian Era,” ca. 1850, was restored by Barry Ruderman and Alex Clausen of Ruderman Antique Maps in the early 2020s.
0437-Peabody-15895000.creditLine: Image courtesy of the David Rumsey Map Collection, Cartography Associates.
0437-Peabody-15895000.digitizedLine: Digitized by the David Rumsey Map Collection, Cartography Associates.
0437-Peabody-15895000.altText:
A historical chronological chart titled "CHRISTIAN ERA" displaying a comprehensive timeline from year 1 to 2000 CE. The chart is organized in a grid format with 20 panels (4 rows × 5 columns), each representing 100-year periods. Each panel contains a 10×10 grid of squares, with each square representing one year. The panels have bold black borders. 
The panels are numbered in the corners (1-100, 101-200, 201-300, etc., up to 1901-2000), and significant historical events, dates, and names are written within the appropriate year squares throughout the timeline. The chart uses different colored squares to highlight important years or periods - some squares appear in red, green, and other colors against the predominant beige/tan background. Text in all capitals is stenciled in, and includes references to CRUSADES, PROTESTANT,  HELVETIC CONFEDERACY, GENGHIS KHAN and various ruler names, religious events, and other historical milestones scattered throughout the appropriate time periods.
